title: Scripture is the analytic, proper, spiritual principle that settles controversy; without analytic ministry no spiritual proof
pass_a_gloss: This is an analytic principle, οἰκεῖον, vernacular, spiritual, by which every theological and spiritual controversy is to be settled. For just as from the analytics, indeed from the whole philosophy of Aristotle, Plato and of others also, even if such things are pounded in a mortar, a unique spiritual proof cannot be expressed and elicited for confirming the articles of faith, nor can the spiritual errors of the Arians, Pontificals and other sectaries be solidly refuted: so on the contrary it is most truly said that without the ministry of analytic doctrine, which admits nothing in theology except what is οἰκεῖον proper, vernacular, or presupposed by it in other disciplines, agreeing with spiritual things and analogous to the faith (for this is ἀναλύειν in theology, 1 Cor. 2:13), which either by the goodness of nature befalls excellent talents — though only to very few and in an imperfect mode — or more firmly, from a stronger principle, namely is granted by the Holy Spirit to some, as to the Apostles, in a more divine mode, or finally is acquired by precepts and teaching; which is a surer guide than nature — that the truth of no controversy can accurately and solidly be proved, taught, known, or its falsity struck down and confuted, whether that controversy has been stirred in philosophy or in theology. For on both sides it warns that proper principles must be used for proving the proper theorems of a discipline — philosophical for philosophical things, theological for theological. For only in this way can and ought philosophical things to be treated philosophically, and theological things theologically.
pass_b_english: This is an analytic principle — proper (οἰκεῖον), native to the discipline, and spiritual — by which every theological and spiritual controversy is to be decided. For just as from the analytics, or even from the whole philosophy of Aristotle, Plato, and others, though you pound such learning in a mortar, you still cannot draw out and elicit a single spiritual proof to confirm the articles of faith, nor solidly refute the spiritual errors of the Arians, the papal party, and other sectaries — so, on the other side, it is most truly said that without the ministry of analytic doctrine, which admits into theology nothing but what is proper (οἰκεῖον) and native, or what theology itself presupposes in other disciplines as agreeing with spiritual things and analogous to the faith (for this is to analyze, ἀναλύειν, in theology, [[1 Corinthians 2:13 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:13]]), no controversy's truth can be accurately and solidly proved, taught, or known, nor its falsity struck down and confuted — whether the dispute has been raised in philosophy or in theology.

That analytic gift either falls to excellent natural talents — though only to a few, and imperfectly — or more firmly, from a stronger principle, is granted by the Holy Spirit to some, as to the Apostles, in a more divine mode, or finally is acquired by precepts and teaching; and that teaching is a surer guide than nature. On both sides we are warned to use proper principles for proving the proper theorems of a discipline — philosophical principles for philosophical things, theological for theological. Only so can and should philosophical matters be treated philosophically, and theological matters theologically.
source_text: Hoc est principium analyticum, οἰκεῖον, vernaculum, spirituale, quo omnis controversia theologica & spiritualis dirimenda est. Quemadmodum enim ex analyticis, imo e tota philosophia Aristotelis, Platonis & aliorum etiam, qua talium vel in mortario contusa, non potest unica probatio spiritualis exprimi & elici ad confirmandum articulos fidei, neque Arianorum, Pontificiorum & aliorum sectariorum spirituales errores solide refutari: ita ex adverso verissime dicitur, sine ministerio analyticae doctrinae, quae nihil admittit in theologia nisi οἰκεῖον proprium, vernaculum, aut ab ea in aliis disciplinis praesuppositum, rebus spiritualibus consentaneum & fidei analogum (hoc enim est ἀναλύειν in theologia 1. Cor. 2.13.) quae vel bonitate naturae excellentibus ingeniis, quamvis admodum paucis & imperfecto tantum modo contingit, vel καρτερικωτέρως, a fortiori principio, nimirum a Spiritu sancto nonnullis tribuitur, ut Apostolis, modo diviniore, vel denique praeceptis & doctrina comparatur; quae certior dux est quam natura, nullius controversiae veritatem accurate, solideque probari, doceri, cognosci, aut falsitatem elidi, confutarique posse, sive ea controversia in philosophia, sive in theologia sit excitata. Utrobique enim monet utendum esse propriis principiis ad propria disciplinae theoremata probanda, philosophicis ad philosophica, theologicis ad theologica. Hoc enim duntaxat modo philosophica philosophice, theologica theologice tractari possunt & debent.
